KEY MESSAGE 1...Dry and cool weather through Tuesday night. Breezy, 
especially across Cape Cod and the Islands. 

Anomalous 1030+ mb high pressure over southeast Ontario Monday, 
builds eastward into Quebec Tuesday, providing dry and cool weather 
for Southern New England through at least Tue night. Northeast 
gradient will maintain breezy conditions, especially across 
southeast MA, including Cape Cod and Islands. Model soundings here 
support NE winds 15-20 mph with gusts up to 25 mph at times, less 
wind away from the coastline. 

Abundant sunshine Monday afternoon, except post frontal strato-cu 
over southeast MA from departing frontal wave, combined with cool 
northeast flow over the relatively mild ocean. Mid/high clouds will 
preclude radiational cooling tonight, but a very dry airmass (dew 
pts in the 40s and 50s) will be sufficient for min temps to fall 
into 40s, except low to mid 50s along the coast, including metro 
Boston, Providence and Hartford.

Tuesday, short wave over the OH valley today spreads mid/high clouds 
into SNE tonight and Tue. However mid level confluent flow over the 
region will provide sufficient subsidence for dry weather to 
prevail. These mid/high clouds will yield filtered sunshine Tue. 
Cooler temps aloft (+7C to +9C) combined with subsidence inversion 
from 1030+ mb high, will yield another day of cooler than normal 
highs Tue, with highs only in the low to mid 60s, about 10 degs 
below normal. 

KEY MESSAGE 2...Mainly dry and cool conditions persist through 
mid- week. Monitoring potential late-week coastal low that has 
potential to bring rain, strong winds, and coastal impacts 
depending on the track. 

Ensemble guidance remains in good agreement that an anomalously
strong surface high will set up over Quebec and persist through
late week. This will advect in a below normal airmass, yielding
high temperatures in the upper 50s and 60s alongside a prolonged
period of northeasterly flow through the week. A weak low
pressure system moves through the Mid-Atlantic on Tuesday. 
There remains uncertainty regarding its northern extent; 
however, if it tracks north enough, a few light showers are 
possible. The higher probabilities for any showers will be for 
CT, south coast, and Cape/Islands. Otherwise, expect mainly dry 
conditions through mid-week. 

Attention turns to a developing coastal low late in the week.
Deterministic and ensemble guidance continues to highlight a
slow-moving low developing and tracking northward toward the
northeast coast by late-week. However, considerable spread
remains in the exact track and strength of the low. Ensemble
means have largely settled on a middle-ground solutions of the
low developing off the Mid-Atlantic coast Wednesday, followed by
a northward track into closer proximity of southern New England
Thursday and Friday. Looking at individual members, tracks range
from as far west as Long Island to near Cape Cod, to further
offshore southeast or east of southern New England. Recent ECMWF
ensemble runs have exhibited subtle shifts east/west in the
cluster of low tracks, while the GEFS has show a subtle but
consistent trend west. Regardless of the exact track, ensemble
means bring the low close enough to bring strong gusts, rain,
and coastal impacts(erosion/coastal flooding). It is important
to note that the exact track and low strength will strongly 
influence the magnitude of gusts, QPF, and how far inland the
rain extends. 

While the center of the low likely holds off until late week,
marine and coastal impacts may begin as early as Wednesday. As
the low deepens in the Mid-Atlantic, the robust high to the
north will aid in tightening the regional pressure gradient,
particularly across the southern coastal waters. This will
support development of strong winds by Wednesday AM, well ahead
of the primary low. The exact positioning and strength the
associated areas of high/low pressure will dictate how strong
the winds could be. There is growing confidence in Gale
force(40mph+) for the southern coastal waters which has been
heavily supported by the ECMWF and its ensemble, though the
GEFS/GFS remain slightly weaker. A Gale Watch has been issued in
these areas. As the system lifts northward expect strong gusts
to continue if not strengthen and expand across portions of the
waters. The ECMWF ensemble even shows low probabilities 
(10-25%) for greater than 45 mph gusts Thursday into Friday. 
Inland winds will also be gusty, though lighter than over the 
waters with gusts 25-35 mph, strongest along the immediate 
coast. 

This prolonged period of gusty northeasterly winds will build
rough seas and elevate the threat for coastal erosion and
flooding depending on the track. Given the aforementioned spread
in track and intensity across models, rain amounts have also
remained uncertain. Most guidance suggests the rain shield will
clip at least the far eastern portions of MA with the 50th and
upper percentiles shifting the shield further west.
